title: Branching Gaps, Coexistence, and Boundary Influence for the Ising Model on Spherically Symmetric Trees
abstract: In this paper, we study the ferromagnetic nearest-neighbor Ising model on rooted spherically symmetric trees with one or \(q\) children per vertex, according to a prescribed sequence of branching levels. Unbounded runs of one-child levels force uniqueness at every nonzero homogeneous field and every finite inverse temperature. We quantify this effect through the locations of sufficiently long nonbranching stretches. Conversely, uniqueness need not entail any uniform rate: for each prescribed vanishing sequence, we construct a density-one tree whose finite-volume boundary influence decays more slowly along a subsequence. The tree retains branching number \(q\), although its nonzero-field coexistence region disappears. For eventually bounded gaps, we prove an optimal uniform comparison with the periodic tree having the largest allowed gap and obtain an explicit interval of coexistence fields. Thus bounded gaps are equivalent, within this family, to coexistence at some finite temperature and nonzero field. For eventually periodic gaps, Gibbs uniqueness is equivalent to fixed-point uniqueness of the full-period return map. A negative Schwarzian derivative yields a complete classification: in the supercritical regime the map has three fixed points inside a closed coexistence interval, two at its endpoints, and one outside. The nonzero endpoints are automatically nondegenerate folds, with square-root splitting of the merging branches.
summary: This work mathematically analyzes the Ising model on structured trees to determine when its Gibbs measure is unique or when phase coexistence occurs. It establishes a deep link between the geometry of the tree (specifically, the pattern of branching gaps) and the physical properties of the model. The results provide precise conditions for uniqueness, showing that unbounded gaps enforce uniqueness, while bounded gaps allow for a non-trivial coexistence region.
main_problem: The paper investigates the relationship between the geometric structure of a graph (specifically, spherically symmetric trees with varying branching gaps) and the physical properties of the Ising model, such as Gibbs measure uniqueness and field coexistence.
main_result: Unbounded runs of one-child levels force the Ising model to have a unique Gibbs measure for any non-zero external field, while the existence of a non-zero coexistence region implies that the gaps must be bounded.
method: The analysis employs cavity recursion relations, contraction mapping principles, and comparisons between the model on structured trees and regular lattices to establish rigorous mathematical criteria for phase transitions.
model_or_system: The system is the ferromagnetic nearest-neighbor Ising model studied on rooted spherically symmetric trees. The Hamiltonian includes nearest-neighbor couplings, external fields, and is analyzed via its finite-volume Gibbs measure.
key_observables: Gibbs measure uniqueness, the field coexistence region, and the rate of boundary influence decay ($\Delta_N(H)$).
important_parameters: Inverse temperature ($ eta$), coupling constant ($J$), external field ($H$), and the branching structure defined by gap sequences ($\alpha$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to leafless, spherically symmetric trees with offspring numbers limited to $\{1, q\}$ ($q \ge 2$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing general uniqueness criteria based on gap structure, then providing specific theorems for unbounded and bounded gaps, and finally analyzing the equivalence between uniqueness and fixed-point properties for periodic gaps.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the rigorous mathematical techniques involving recursive relations, contraction mappings, and phase transition criteria are foundational tools applicable to analyzing quantum phase transitions or quantum field theories on structured lattices.
